lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 5, why check a fact in two sources? (If they agree, you can trust it more.) Today: research a question, judge your sources, take notes in your own words and list where your facts came from.
Start with a clear question you can research: "How do bees make honey?" Then gather information from several sources: books, trusted websites, encyclopedias, museums and experts you ask.

Judge each source: is it reliable? Ask who the author is (an expert?) and when it was written (up to date?). Ask why (to inform, or to sell?) and whether other sources agree. A comment under a video is not reliable.
Take notes in your own words: read a part, close the book, then write the key facts as short notes. Keep the source beside each note, so you can check it later.
A paraphrase says an idea in your own words and your own sentence shape, keeping the meaning. "Bees turn nectar into honey in the hive" becomes "In the hive, nectar is made into honey by bees."
Copying someone's words or ideas and pretending they are yours is plagiarism, and it is unfair to the writer. If you use exact words, put them in speech marks as a quote and say who wrote them.
At the end, list your sources in alphabetical order of the authors' surnames: the author, the year, the title and where you found it, so readers can check your facts.

Try it in the world: with a grown-up, research one question about an animal in two books or trusted websites. Write five notes in your own words, a source for each, and a short source list. Next: discuss and present.

exercises.prompt: Which source is most reliable for facts about volcanoes?
choices: a book by a volcano scientist
exercises.hint: Who knows the subject best?
exercises.explain: A scientist who studies volcanoes is an expert, so their book is reliable.

exercises.prompt: Copying a paragraph and handing it in as your own work is plagiarism.
exercises.hint: Whose words are they?
exercises.explain: True: using someone's words or ideas without saying so is plagiarism.

exercises.prompt: What is a paraphrase?
choices: an idea in your own words, same meaning
exercises.hint: The same idea, told another way.
exercises.explain: A paraphrase keeps the meaning but uses your own words and sentence shape.

exercises.prompt: You want to use a writer's exact words. What must you do?
choices: put them in speech marks and name the writer
exercises.hint: Show the reader they are not your words.
exercises.explain: Quote the exact words, in speech marks, and say who wrote them.

exercises.prompt: Put the research steps in order.
items: take notes in your own words
exercises.hint: Start with the question; end with the source list.
exercises.explain: Ask a question, find sources, take notes in your own words, write it up, then list your sources.

exercises.prompt: Which is the best research question?
exercises.hint: Can facts from sources answer it?
exercises.explain: "How do bees make honey?" is clear, and facts from sources can answer it.

exercises.prompt: The source says: "Honeybees dance to show where food is." Which note is in your own words?
choices: bees: a dance points to food
Honeybees dance to show where food is.
exercises.hint: A note uses your own short words, not a copy.
exercises.explain: "bees: a dance points to food" keeps the fact in your own words; the first choice is copied.

exercises.prompt: Two books give different numbers of bees in a hive. What should you do?
exercises.hint: When sources disagree, look further.
exercises.explain: Check other trusted sources; if they still disagree, say that sources give different numbers.

exercises.prompt: Sort the sources: reliable, or not reliable, for a school report?
exercises.hint: Ask who wrote it and why.
exercises.explain: Reliable: a museum's website, an encyclopedia, a book by an expert. Not reliable: a joke website, an advert, a stranger's post.

exercises.prompt: Put the source list in order: A to Z by the author's surname.
exercises.hint: Look at the first letter of each surname.
exercises.explain: Adams, Brown, Okafor, Silva: A to Z.

exercises.prompt: An advert from a sweet company is a reliable source about healthy eating.
exercises.hint: Why was it written?
exercises.explain: False: it was written to sell, so it may leave out facts that do not help sales.

exercises.prompt: Where did the note "a hive has one queen" come from?
exercises.hint: Read across the row.
exercises.explain: The table keeps each note beside its source: Okafor, 2019.

exercises.prompt: Which is the best paraphrase of: "Sharks can sense tiny electric fields made by animals."
choices: Sharks feel the faint electricity of animals.
Sharks can sense tiny electric fields.
exercises.hint: The same meaning in new words: no copying, no changed facts, no opinions.
exercises.explain: It keeps the meaning in new words; the others copy, change the fact or add an opinion.

exercises.prompt: Why do you list your sources at the end?
choices: so readers can check your facts
exercises.hint: Who might want to find where a fact came from?
exercises.explain: A source list lets readers check your facts, and it gives credit to the writers.

exercises.prompt: Which source is most up to date for the number of people in a city?
choices: a story set in the city
exercises.hint: The number of people changes every year.
exercises.explain: Populations change, so the newest official count is the most reliable.

exercises.prompt: Changing a few words in a copied paragraph makes it your own work.
exercises.hint: Whose ideas and sentence shape are they still?
exercises.explain: False: it is still plagiarism; read, close the source, and write the idea in your own words and shape.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is plagiarism?
choices: copying a friend's report and signing it
quoting a writer and naming them
asking an expert and saying so
exercises.hint: Which one hides where the words came from?
exercises.explain: Copying and signing someone else's work passes it off as yours; the others give credit.

exercises.prompt: A website has no author, no date and lots of adverts. What should you do?
choices: trust it because it is online
exercises.hint: What makes a source reliable?
exercises.explain: Without an author or a date you cannot judge it, so look for a better source.

exercises.prompt: Match each question about a source to what it checks.
matches: if it is up to date
if the author is an expert
exercises.hint: Card 2 lists four questions to ask about every source.
exercises.explain: Who: is the author an expert? When: is it up to date? Why: to inform, or to sell? Do others agree: does it match other sources?

exercises.prompt: Sort the ways of using a source: fair, or plagiarism?
items: quoting with speech marks and a name
copying a page as your own
changing a few words of a copied page
exercises.hint: Does the writer get credit, and are the words really yours?
exercises.explain: Fair: a quote in speech marks with the writer's name, a paraphrase with the source listed, notes in your own words. Plagiarism: copying a page as yours, or changing a few words of a copied page.

exercises.prompt: A new source list: order it A to Z by the authors' surnames.
exercises.hint: Look only at the first letter of each surname.
exercises.explain: Baker, Evans, Mendes, Zhou: B, E, M, Z. In an A to Z list, readers can find any source quickly.

exercises.prompt: Your report uses facts from 3 books and 2 websites, and a quote from 1 expert you asked. How many sources go in your list?
exercises.hint: Every place a fact or a quote came from goes in the list.
exercises.explain: 3 books, 2 websites and 1 expert: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 sources. Every source of a fact or a quote is listed, so readers can check them.
